hints: Look at what is building up in the soil. More dissolved salt means more solute, so think about what that does to the water potential of the soil solution.
Remember the golden rule: water always moves by osmosis from higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) water potential. Compare soil to root.
walkthrough:
**What does extra salt do to soil water?**

Adding solute always lowers water potential, making it more negative. So as salt builds up, the water potential in the soil decreases.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{more solute} \rightarrow \text{lower (more negative) } \Psi$$

**Which way will water move now?**

Normally soil $\Psi$ is higher than root $\Psi$, so water moves into the roots. After salinisation, soil $\Psi$ becomes lower than root $\Psi$.

Water moves down the gradient:
$$\text{high } \Psi \text{ (roots)} \rightarrow \text{low } \Psi \text{ (salty soil)}$$

**Link to the plant dying**

That means water is drawn out of the roots by osmosis instead of into them. The plant cannot take up water for photosynthesis and turgor, so it wilts and eventually dies. That matches row C perfectly.

options.A: The direction is correct, but the location is wrong. It is the soil water potential that decreases due to salt, not the root water potential.
options.B: This is backwards. An increase in root water potential with water moving in would help the plant take up water, not kill it.
options.C: Extra salt lowers (decreases) soil water potential below that of the roots, so water moves out of the roots by osmosis and the plant dies from water loss.
options.D: Adding salt cannot increase soil water potential. Solutes always lower water potential, so this row gets the principle the wrong way round.
